chapter_theme: Last songs at Palani (பழநி, 7 of 7), several at Avinankudi: the poet sets knowing Murugan above alchemy, traces his life from the womb to ruin among women, lists the body's diseases and the cheats around it, sees women's beauty as maya in form, and asks for the feet, for tears of devotion and for the simple rite of pouring Ganges water on them.
structure_note: A short song against alchemy (194); a life from womb to waste (195); disease and the false body (196); desire seen as maya (197); confessions of desire with pleas for the feet (198 to 200), 200 asking for puja. Murugan as Siva's or Brahma's teacher appears in 196, 197 and 200.

194.reading: A short song: if one realises that Murugan, the giver of boons, is the gem, what will not come; it does not come by mercury and the like, for the nine metals put in turn to charcoal, so what use is that? The praise names him the son of the supreme Goddess whom the Vedas, Brahma, Vishnu and all the Agamas do not know, Lord of Palani.
194.nuance: இரதாதிகளால் நவலோகம் இடவே கரியாம் seems to reject the alchemist's art: mercury (இரதம்) and the nine metals give only charcoal, while the true gem is Murugan himself. The reading depends on how the clipped short lines divide, so it is tentative.

195.reading: The poet traces his life: heated in a woman's body, rolling in blood, long in the womb, born in human form, growing daily to sixteen, then wandering in the nets of women, embracing them, seeking wealth and losing it all, lost in infatuation, and asks Murugan to rule him by grace. The praise names him the lover of the millet-field girl given by Vishnu (Raghunatha), son of Siva who burned Kama and of the Goddess called Matangi, Kumari, Nili and Chandi, who destroyed the asuras and freed the gods, at Palani.
195.nuance: The life runs in a single sentence from the womb (வனிதை உடல் காய நின்று உதிரமதிலே உருண்டு) to ruin, with sixteen as the age when the body takes its shape and the trouble begins. பொருள்தேடி... கனபொருள் எலாம் இழந்து: the wealth he gathered was lost in the women's nets. புனமதனில் வாழுகின்ற வநிதை ரகுநாதர் தந்த புதல்வி makes Valli Vishnu's daughter.

196.reading: The poet lists the body's diseases, wind, bile, phlegm, colic, dropsy, eye disease, piles, cough and vomiting, and the ninety-six tattvas and the cheats who live around a man, and confesses that, with the three cravings, he took this thieving, false hut for happiness and ran in fine cloth and gold chains as if to outrun the seven worlds; he asks to reach the feet of the Lord's pure devotees. The praise sounds the battle drums as the vel shakes Adisesha, the seas and the asura hill, tells how Murugan struck Brahma's golden head and as true guru spoke in Siva's ear the gain of the detached, and how he went in disguise after Valli, at Palani.
196.nuance: பொய்க்குடில், the false hut, is the body, and the list of diseases is the evidence. தத்துவகாரர் தொண்ணூற்றறுவர் treats the ninety-six tattvas as agents who crowd the body. The teaching myth is told in full except for the word Om: வேதன் பொற்சிரம் மீது கடாவி, நல் ஈசன் சற்குருவாய் அவர் காதினில் மேவும் பற்றிலர் பேறு அருள் ஓதிய. The opening lines on the drums (தீதந் தித்திமி, டுடுண் டுட்டுடு) are rhythm, not words.

197.reading: The poet describes a woman, breasts like an elephant's brow under necklaces, face like the young moon, long carp eyes, nectar lips, plantain thighs, thread-thin waist, the gait of a peacock and swan, and asks that the understanding arise in him that this deceit is great maya itself standing in form. The praise names the vel that destroyed the night-walkers so Indra could rule, the son of Siva who drank the poison for the gods, the one who argued with Brahma, asked him for one word he could not give, and broke his pride by confinement, at towered Avinankudi.
197.nuance: தோதகந்தனை மாமாயையே வடிவாக நின்றது: the plea asks not to escape the woman but to see her charm as maya embodied, a doctrinal turn on the usual confession. The Brahma story (ஆரணன்றனை வாதாடி ஓர் உரை ஓதுகின்றென வாராது) is told without naming Om.

198.reading: The poet describes women with flower-garlanded hair who speak of love, generosity and their own pride, with golden, Meru-like breasts that seek battle, walking swan-like in the street and deluding all with the net of their eyes, and asks that his mind not wither but that one day Murugan rule him by his two lotus feet. The praise names the vel that split Sura in two, the son of Uma called Narani, Gauri, Syamala, Parvati, Mauna Sundari and Yogini, who circles the seven worlds in an instant on the peacock, at Palani, said to surpass Kasi, shining like ten million suns.
198.nuance: எனை யாள்வதும் ஒருநாளே: the plea is put as a hope for one day. காசியின் மீறிய பழநி, Palani above Kasi, claims for the shrine more than the holiest pilgrim city.

199.reading: The poet describes women in the bed of desire, hair falling, eyes rolling, words faltering, whom he sought night and day until his heart's knowledge was gone, and asks that, the darkness lifted, he wear Murugan's anklet feet on his head, weep and weep for his grace and proclaim his sweet praise. The praise names him nephew of Vishnu sleeping on the serpent beside Lakshmi, the vel that plunged into the asuras' fat and freed the gods, and son of Siva who drank the poison and bears the Ganga, at Palani.
199.nuance: அழுதழுது உன் அருள் விரும்பி: the remedy is tears, devotion shown in the body that desire had seized. The feet are asked for on the head (எனது தலைமிசை அணிந்து), as a crown.

200.reading: The poet confesses that he embraced women with bamboo-like shoulders, did sins in vain, wandered far, his mind scattered and his life withered, and asks that, his delusion gone, he pour Ganges water on Murugan's two lotus feet, bow to them and perform some puja. The praise names Rama who burned Lanka and cut off Ravana's heads as his uncle, the vel that killed Sura so the gods could rule, the Goddess as Sundari, Nili, Kundali and Veda Tantri on Siva's left, and Murugan who gladly gave a teaching when Siva, who drank the poison, bowed to him, at Avinankudi.
200.nuance: The plea is modest and ritual: some puja (பூசையும் சிலவே), with Ganges water poured on the feet. ஆலமுண்ட அரனார் இறைஞ்ச ஒர் போதகந்தனையே உகந்து அருள் is the teaching of Siva, without naming Om.

links.note: Both set the Lord above the alchemist's work. Tirumular makes the five-letter mantra the alchemist's pill that turns the body to gold; 194 says mercury and the nine metals end as charcoal, while knowing Murugan as the gem brings everything.
Both tell the poet's life as one arc from the womb and the breast to the houses of women. 181 adds Brahma sending the soul out to eat its deeds; 195 adds the age of sixteen and the wealth lost.
Both make weeping the sign of devotion: Tirumular melts in love and cries day and night, and 199 asks to wear the feet on his head and weep and weep for grace.
Both songs of Avinankudi call Murugan the giver of போதகம், the teaching: 179 opens by hailing him as such, and 200 ends with Siva bowing to receive it.

Thiruppugazh 195 runs a single life from the womb (வனிதையுடல் காய நின்று உதிரமதிலே உருண்டு) through youth to ruin in women's nets and only then asks for grace. Tirumanthiram 487 says that one born of two who met for pleasure and grown in painful bondage (துன்புறு பாசத்தில் தோன்றி வளர்ந்தபின்) can still seek the Ancient and chant him. The mantra states as a general possibility what the song enacts as one man's late plea (உன்றன் அருள்தாராய்).

Thiruppugazh 196 names the ninety-six tattvas as agents crowding the body (தத்துவகாரர் தொண்ணூற்றறுவர்) and calls the body a thieving, false hut (சோரம் பொய்க்குடில்). Tirumanthiram 154 counts the same ninety-six as dwellers in a walled temple (முப்பதும் முப்பதும் முப்பத்தறுவரும்) who all run off once it falls. Both picture the tattvas as tenants of a house that does not last: the mantra as a temple that falls, the song as a false hut.

Both songs open with a physician's list of the body's diseases: 196 has வாதம் பித்தம் ... ஈளைகள் ... மூல வியாதிகள், 894 has வாதமொடு பித்த மூல ... ஈளை. 196 then calls the body a false hut (பொய்க்குடில்) and 894 a ruined body (பாழுடல்) Brahma built, and both ask not to waste life carrying it. The two songs, far apart in the book, are near-repeats of one complaint.

Thiruppugazh 197 opens by likening a woman's breasts to an elephant (வாரணந்தனை நேரான மாமுலை) and goes on to ask that he see her whole charm as great maya in form (மாமாயையே வடிவாக நின்றது). Kural 1087 has the lover compare the cloth over her firm breasts to the face-cloth on a rutting elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேல் கட்படாம்). The same elephant figure is the Kural lover's wonder and, in the song, the first item of an inventory the poet asks to see through.

Thiruppugazh 198 describes women whose breasts seek battle and whose eye-nets delude all, and asks that his mind not wither under them (எனது சிந்தையும் வாடிவிடாவகை) but be ruled by the feet. Tirumanthiram 2141 says desire rising at the waist and a mind sunk at the breast (முலைவாய நெஞ்சத்து மூழ்கும்) send one wandering, while a mind made firm as stone stands before Siva (சிலையாய சித்தம் சிவமுன்). Both set the mind drowned in the woman's body against the mind held before the Lord; the mantra states as a rule what the song asks for.

Thiruppugazh 199 asks to wear the anklet feet on his head and, weeping and weeping, long for grace (அழுதழுது உன் அருள் விரும்பி). Tirumanthiram 43 says the Lord fills and gives his feet to those who speak of Hara's feet crying and weeping (அரற்றி அழுது) and meditate daily on them. Both make tears joined to the feet the way to grace; the song asks for the very state the mantra promises.

Thiruppugazh 200, after a life wasted on women, asks only to pour Ganges water on the two lotus feet, bow and do some little puja (பூசையும் சிலவே புரிந்திட). Tirumanthiram 252 says that anyone can give God a green leaf (யாவர்க்குமாம் இறைவற்கு ஒரு பச்சிலை). Both set the measure of worship low: water and a leaf are enough, and the song's modest plea fits the mantra's claim that such worship is within everyone's reach.

source_issues: Song 196: one corrupt character in தொணு஡றறு (line 8), probably தொண்ணூற்றறு, 'ninety-six'.
